_comment: Hindu expansion 175-drive I: Ramayana episodes A (Griffith 1870-74, public domain).

title.zh: 曼陀羅的耳語與凱凱伊的恩諾

region.zh: 阿逾陀，內廷（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Ayodhya Kanda, Manthara episode

summary.en: On the eve of Rama's consecration, the hunchbacked maid Manthara talked Queen Kaikeyi out of her joy in ten minutes: her son Bharata would be a servant to Rama's crown. The two boons the king owed her from a battlefield - Bharata's throne, and Rama's fourteen years in the forest - were cashed that night, and the ideal reign was destroyed by a hairstyle's worth of vanity.
summary.zh: 羅摩加冕前夕，駝背侍女曼陀羅在十分鐘內說動了正為之歡喜的凱凱伊王后：其子婆羅多將為羅摩王冠之僕。國王於戰場上所欠的二項恩諾——婆羅多即位、羅摩流放十四年——當夜兌現，而理想之治毀於髮式般的虛榮。

passages.text: Kaikeyi was dressed for joy - jewels for the consecration she thought her own son's day - when Manthara, the crooked-backed nurse, asked what she was celebrating; told, she threw down her ornament in a heap. The nurse's arithmetic: a mother's joy is her son's crown; a king's promise is a debtor's silence. Kaikeyi, told that Bharata would serve where he might reign, let the poison finish its work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boons were spoken in the anger-chamber, with the queen lying on the floor like a rejected petitioner: Bharata to the throne, Rama to the forest in bark garments - and the epic's engine was started by a maid with a grudge and a queen with a memory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.en: Bharata and the Sandals of Rama

region.zh: 難提伽羅摩，阿逾陀城外（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Ayodhya Kanda, Bharata's regency

summary.en: Bharata returned from his uncle's court to find a grieving city and a mother's crime done in his name. He chased Rama into the forest to give the throne back; Rama refused - a father's word was a father's word. So Bharata set Rama's sandals on the throne and governed from a hut outside Ayodhya for fourteen years, a regent who treated a pair of shoes as his king.
summary.zh: 婆羅多自舅家歸來，見城內舉哀，母親之罪假其名而行。他追入森林欲還其王位；羅摩不允——父親之言即是王命。於是婆羅多將羅摩之履置於王座，在阿逾陀城外的草廬中攝政十四年，以一雙鞋為其王。

passages.text: Bharata's grief was double: the crown he was given was stolen goods, and the mother who stole it for him had emptied a city's joy - he refused the consecration and rode after his brother. In the forest Rama stood by the dead king's word: the exile was the promise, and a promise made to a queen in love is still a promise; the throne would keep for fourteen years. The compromise became the legend: Rama's sandals set upon the throne-cushion, and Bharata ruling not from the palace but from Nandigrama's hut, hair unbound, bark-garbed - a king dressed as an ascetic serving a pair of shoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

region.zh: 彌提羅，遮那迦之田（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Bala Kanda, Sita's birth

summary.en: King Janaka, ploughing the sacrificial ground, found a girl in the turned earth - a child as bright as a rising dawn, and he raised her as his daughter, naming her Sita, 'furrow'. The earth is her mother in the epic's own words, and the marriage-contest that Shiva's bow decides will break the bow instead.
summary.zh: 遮那迦王於祭祀之地上犁田，於翻起的土中得一女——明亮如初升朝霞的孩子——他養為己女，名之悉多，『犁溝』。史詩自言大地即其母；而決定其婚姻的濕婆神弓，最終被折斷。

passages.text: Janaka was the plough-king of Mithila, and as he turned the first furrow of the sacred ground a child lay in the clods, bright as the dawn that was still in the sky. He lifted her from the earth and called her Sita - furrow - daughter of the ground he tilled; and the princess of the plough grew up in the palace with her origin kept in her name. The earth-mother of the epic is not a metaphor: at the poem's end the ground will open to receive her back - the furrow keeps its child from first page to last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda and Uttara Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.en: The Death of Tataka the Yakshi

region.zh: 多吒迦之林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Bala Kanda, Tataka episode

summary.en: The forest that ate seers was ruled by Tataka, a yakshi cursed into a giant rakshasi's body. Vishvamitra led the teenage princes against her, with a logic he had to argue twice: a rakshasi may not be killed by a god's bolt - the deed belongs to a man. Rama's first arrows blinded her, his second flight cut her down, and the seers' fires burned unrobbed from that evening.
summary.zh: 吞食仙人的森林由多吒迦所轄——一位被詛咒為巨大羅剎女的夜叉。維什瓦米陀引少年王子前往，並須兩次論證其邏輯：羅剎女不可由神杵誅殺——此事屬於人。羅摩的第一輪箭使其盲目，第二輪將其斬落；自此仙人祭火不再被劫。

passages.text: Tataka's story was a curse with a history: a yakshi of beauty, turned by a seer's word into a hill-sized demoness whose appetite emptied the hermitages of the district. Vishvamitra's law was stated like a rule of the hunt: no god's weapon may end her; this is a man's work - and Rama, a boy with his first great bow, was told the theology of manhood before his first battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: She came storming like a thundercloud; his first volley took her eyes, and in her blindness the second rained down and ended the forest's terror - the seers lit their fires that night without robbers at the edge of the light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.zh: 首哩薄那迦的求婚與毀容

region.zh: 哥達瓦里河畔般折婆提（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, Surpanakha episode

summary.en: The rakshasa princess Surpanakha found the exiles in the forest and proposed herself - to Rama, then to Lakshmana, with honest appetite. The brothers' answer was the epic's cruelest prank: she came back mutilated, nose and ears cut by Lakshmana's blade, and her wounded vanity summoned her brother Ravana to avenge the honor no court would give her.
summary.zh: 羅剎女公主首哩薄那迦在林中遇見流亡者，先向羅摩、再向羅什曼那求婚，態度坦率。兄弟的回答是史詩中最殘忍的惡作劇：她毀容而歸——鼻與耳被羅什曼那之刃割去——她受創的虛榮召來兄長羅波那，為任何廷堂都不肯給她的名譽復仇。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; gendered violence readings contested; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Surpanakha, sister of the lord of Lanka, saw the two exiled princes in the forest and offered herself first to Rama, then to Lakshmana - a proposal made with a demoness's frankness and refused with a mortal's caution. The prank that answered her was Lakshmana's blade: she flew at Sita and was cut - nose, ears - and the princes' hunting game sent the mutilated princess home to her brother. Her blood was the fuse of the war: the golden deer, the abduction, Lanka's ruin - the epic's course was set by a proposal nobody bothered to answer decently.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.en: The Golden Deer and Maricha's Last Trick
title.zh: 金鹿與摩哩遮的最後詭計

region.zh: 般折婆提森林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, golden deer episode

summary.en: A deer of gold and jewels stepped into the hermitage clearing - Sita's delight, Rama's warning, and the demon Maricha in disguise. He led Rama leagues into the forest, and dying, imitated Rama's own voice crying for help; Lakshmana left the line only when Sita's anger drove him - and the clearing was empty for Ravana.
summary.zh: 一頭金鑲寶石之鹿踏進仙居空地——悉多所喜、羅摩所疑、實為摩哩遮的偽裝。牠引羅馬深入林中數里，臨死模仿羅摩自己的聲音呼救；羅什曼那只在悉多動怒後才離開界線——空地遂為羅波那讓出。

passages.text: The deer was too beautiful to be real and too real to resist: silver hooves, sapphire eyes, a hide of beaten gold - and Rama went after it with the doubt still in his voice. Maricha led him a whole day's chase and, struck at last, threw his dying voice: Help, Sita, help, Lakshmana - Rama's own accent crying for rescue from the forest's far side. Lakshmana, bound by his brother's order and insulted by his sister-in-law's doubt, drew the line he would break - and the three minutes he was gone were the three minutes that emptied the world of the Ramayana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, Jatayu episode

summary.en: The old vulture Jatayu, friend of Rama's father, saw Ravana's flying chariot cross the sky with Sita inside and attacked it - a bird of years against the ten-headed king of Lanka. He fought until his wings were cut; dying on the rock, he gave Rama the one fact that mattered: she lives; Lanka has her. His pyre was the first Rama lit for an ally.
summary.zh: 老鷹闍吒優私，羅摩之父的故友，見羅波那的飛車載著悉多越過天空，便攻擊之——以垂暮之鳥對抗楞伽的十首之王。戰至翼斷；死於岩上時，他給了羅摩唯一要緊的事實：她活著；楞伽藏她。羅摩為其盟友點燃的第一座火堆屬於他。

passages.text: Jatayu met the abductor in the sky - an old vulture against a flying palace - and held the chariot in the clouds with beak and wing while Sita wept beneath the fight. Ravana cut the wings that held him; the bird fell like a stone among the rocks, and the king of Lanka flew on with his prize - the first casualty of the war, unwitnessed by either army.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: Rama and Lakshmana found the wreck of the bird and heard the report that turned grief into a campaign: she lives, in the southern sea, in Ravana's island - and the pyre of a vulture was the war's first rite.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

region.zh: 丹陀迦森林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, Kabandha episode

summary.en: In the Dandaka the brothers met a monster with no head and a mouth in its belly, arms a league long: Kabandha, a gandharva cursed into the shape, who caught travelers as a bird catches fish. Disarmed by grief at first, they cut off his arms at last, burned him - and the freed spirit rose from the pyre to give them their road-map: Sugriva of Kishkindha, Hanuman, the south.
summary.zh: 在丹陀迦，兄弟們遇見一隻無首而口在腹中、雙臂長達一里路的怪物：迦般陀，被詛咒成此形的乾達婆，如鳥捕魚般捕捉旅人。初因悲痛而失手，終於斬其雙臂，焚其身——被解咒的靈魂自火堆中升起，交給他們整張路線圖：猴王須羯哩婆、哈奴曼、南方。

passages.text: Kabandha's arms were the forest's trap: no head to reason with, a mouth in the belly, and a reach that closed like a net on anything that walked the dark path. When his arms were cut off at last and the body burned, the monster stood up out of the fire as a radiant gandharva - the curse ended by the very death he had forced on travelers. His gift was the plot: go to Kishkindha, to Sugriva the exile monkey-king; the monkey who leaps the ocean waits there - and the search for Sita found its map in a pyre's smoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

region.zh: 般婆湖，黎沙牟迦山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, Shabari episode

summary.en: The old ascetic woman Shabari had kept her master's ashram swept for years, waiting for two guests she had been promised. When Rama came, she fed him berries she had tasted first - the fruit a poor old woman could offer - and he accepted every one. Bhakti's first charter in the Ramayana: the devotional meal offered before the worthy offering.
summary.zh: 年邁的苦行女莎婆利多年來一直灑掃其師之道場，等待她被告知將會來到的兩位客人。羅摩來到時，她奉上自己先嚐過的野果——一位貧苦老婦所能獻出的果實——而他一一受之。奉愛在《羅摩衍那》中的第一份憲章：先於合儀之祭的奉愛之餐。

passages.text: Shabari's ashram had been swept and waiting: her master, dying, had told her that Rama would come, and she kept the fire, the water-pots and the path for years of forest silence. She offered him the berries of the forest, each one tasted first for sweetness - the purest thing she had, given the only way she knew how to give. Rama ate what kings would have refused, and the poem's theology turned in his mouth: devotion outcounts ceremony - the first charter of bhakti hidden in a hunger-strike of an old woman's hospitality.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.en: The Death of Vali, Shot from Cover
title.zh: 婆黎之死：自掩蔽處射出的一箭

region.zh: 猴國吉什金陀（象徵性定位於漢皮）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Kishkindha Kanda, Vali episode

summary.en: Vali, the monkey-king whose strength doubled from any foe he faced, had exiled his brother Sugriva and taken his wife. Rama agreed to help - and shot the king from behind a tree as he fought Sugriva. Dying, Vali asked the question the epic has answered ever since: where was the dharma in a hidden arrow? Rama's answer - the king who took his brother's wife - has satisfied fewer readers than the question.
summary.zh: 猴王婆黎的力量因面對之敵而倍增，曾放逐其弟須羯哩婆並奪其妻。羅摩應允相助——在婆黎與須羯哩婆相鬥時自樹後一箭射之。垂死的婆黎問出史詩至今仍要回答的問題：自掩蔽處放箭，正法何在？羅摩的答案——奪弟之妻之王——說服的讀者遠少於問題本身。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition; the shot's ethics are debated inside the tradition; classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Vali's strength was arithmetic: whatever he fought, he fought twice as strong - no army could beat him front-on, and his brother Sugriva lived only because exile was cheaper than war. The duel with Sugriva had turned once already; as the brothers closed again, an arrow came from the trees where Rama stood hidden, and the invincible king fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

passages.text: His dying argument named the problem: I wronged my brother, judge me in the open - why did the lord of dharma shoot from cover? Rama's answer (the wife taken, the code of allies) closed the case in the poem and reopened it in every retelling since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.
